program_plain: World: a random network of 400 nodes (mean degree 6). Node types: 2 opinions (random start). Rules each step: a random node picks a random neighbour of a different opinion; with probability 0.95 it cuts that link and links to a random node of its own opinion, otherwise it adopts the neighbour's opinion.
model_family: opinion dynamics / adaptive (coevolving) voter model on networks
standard_name: Coevolving/adaptive voter model (rewire-to-same) with fragmentation (absorbing) transition
citations: Vazquez, Eguíluz, San Miguel 2008, Phys. Rev. Lett. 100, 108702 (arXiv:0710.4910) - same rule; absorbing transition at p_c=(mu-2)/(mu-1); frozen phase = fragmented network
Holme & Newman 2006, Phys. Rev. E 74, 056108 - original model, nonequilibrium transition in coevolution of networks and opinions (verified via reference lists only)
Durrett et al. 2012, PNAS 109, 3682-3687 - Graph fission in an evolving voter model; rewire-to-same discontinuous transition, evolution stops when no discordant edges
Gross & Blasius 2008, J. R. Soc. Interface 5, 259-271 - review of adaptive coevolutionary networks (verified via reference lists only)
searches: adaptive voter model network rewiring fragmentation transition Holme Newman coevolution of networks and opinions
Durrett Gleeson Lloyd Mattingly Graph fission in an evolving voter model
Vazquez Eguíluz San Miguel generic absorbing transition coevolution dynamics
notes: With mean degree 6, mean-field p_c=0.8, so p=0.95 and 0.9 are in the fragmented (frozen) phase. Fragmentation would normally give >=2 components with giant fraction ~0.5, so n_giant=1.0 and n_components=-2.0 look inconsistent with the standard outcome unless they are normalised/relative metrics or the run reached global consensus (possible at N=400). Metric definitions should be checked. 'Consensus gain' most likely means local (within-component) agreement.
full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** Two of the three observed features fit the literature. The third, n_giant = 1.0, does not fit the standard fragmented outcome and needs checking.

**1. Model family.** This is the coevolving (adaptive) voter model, in the opinion-dynamics and adaptive-network family. A node copies a neighbour's opinion, or breaks the link to a disagreeing neighbour and rewires to a node that already shares its opinion. This is the "rewire-to-same" version.

**2. The behaviour in the literature.**
- Vazquez, Eguíluz & San Miguel (2008) study exactly this rule. A link between opposite-state nodes is rewired with probability p, while with probability 1-p one of the nodes takes its neighbour's state.
  - A mean-field approximation reveals an absorbing transition from an active to a frozen phase at p_c=(μ-2)/(μ-1), which depends only on the average degree μ.
  - The active and frozen phases correspond to a connected and a fragmented network respectively.
  - For mean degree 6, p_c = 0.8. Both p = 0.95 and p = 0.9 therefore lie in the frozen, fragmented regime.
- Holme & Newman (2006, Phys. Rev. E 74, 056108) introduced the model. I confirmed the title and venue only through reference lists, since the full text was not available.
- Durrett et al. (2012, PNAS 109, 3682) is a close relative. With probability α, x breaks its connection to y and makes a new connection to a voter chosen at random from those that share its opinion. The process continues until there are no edges connecting voters that disagree. They report a discontinuous transition in the rewire-to-same model, similar to that of Holme and Newman.
- A review is Gross & Blasius (2008), "Adaptive coevolutionary networks: a review", J. R. Soc. Interface 5, 259–271. I saw this only in reference lists. A second review-style source I did read is the adaptive-networks overview, which frames the central question as whether the dynamics end in consensus or in fragmentation into two disconnected camps, with the transition between them called the fragmentation transition.

**3. Interpreting the observations.**
- "Consensus gain" is the standard result at high rewiring. The system reaches an absorbing state with no discordant links, so every neighbour pair agrees.
- That agreement is local, within components. The frozen phase corresponds to a fragmented network where each component is in a consensus state.
- Fewer components (n_components = -2.0) is not what I would expect at p = 0.95, which should give at least two components, one per opinion. The sign convention or baseline of that metric is unclear.
- n_giant = 1.0 is more puzzling. If it is the literal giant-component fraction, it contradicts the expected split into roughly equal opinion camps, where the largest component would hold about half the nodes.
  - It would fit only if the metric is a normalised or relative score, or the starting network was not connected.
  - It would also fit a run that ended in global consensus. That is possible in a 400-node system, because a minority can die out before the network splits.
  - I could not resolve this from the description.

**4. Confidence: medium.** The model, the rule, the critical rewiring rate and the fragmentation outcome are all well documented, so the verdict is solid. The ambiguity in the giant-component and component-count metrics keeps it from being high. I also did not find a source that reports those exact metrics at N = 400 and mean degree 6.

- "Durrett Gleeson Lloyd Mattingly Graph fission in an evolving voter model"
- "Vazquez Eguíluz San Miguel generic absorbing transition coevolution dynamics"
